{{< include ../_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

The fable packages are large for a browser, so these exercises practise the ideas of Chapter 15 with functions that come with R: `ts()` for time series, `acf()` for autocorrelation, `stl()` for decomposition, and benchmark forecasts built by hand. The downloadable project at the bottom uses tsibble, fable, and feasts, exactly as in the chapter. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5, ex6]
counselling <- read.csv("counselling_visits.csv")
visits <- ts(counselling$visits, frequency = 52, start = c(2020, 1))
clinic <- c(12, 10, 9, 11, 7, 3, 2,   14, 11, 10, 12, 8, 4, 2)
mae <- function(actual, forecast) mean(abs(actual - forecast))
year_of <- function(k) counselling$visits[(k - 1) * 52 + 1:52]   # academic year k
```

## Benchmarks by hand

### Exercise 1: Three benchmark forecasts

The setup code has created the chapter's clinic series: two weeks of daily visits, starting on a Monday. Calculate the forecasts for the next seven days with the mean, naive, and seasonal naive methods.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
mean_fc   <- rep(mean(clinic), 7)
naive_fc  <- rep(clinic[length(clinic)], 7)
snaive_fc <- clinic[______:14]        # the last full week
rbind(mean_fc, naive_fc, snaive_fc)
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The last full week is the last seven days: days 8 to 14.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
snaive_fc <- clinic[8:14]
```

The same numbers as fable produced in the chapter: 8.2 every day for the mean, 2 every day for the naive method (the last Sunday), and last week's pattern for the seasonal naive method.
:::
:::

## Patterns

### Exercise 2: A time plot

`visits` is a `ts` object, R's built-in time series format, with 52 observations per year (`frequency = 52`). Plot it, and add a horizontal line at the average.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
plot(visits, ylab = "Visits per week", xlab = "Year of the series")
abline(h = mean(______), lty = "dashed")
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
abline(h = mean(visits), lty = "dashed")
```

The series swings far above and below its average every year: a forecast of the average would be badly wrong most of the time. The time axis counts years from the start of the series, 2020.
:::
:::

### Exercise 3: Autocorrelation

Calculate the autocorrelation of the series at lags 1 and 52. (`acf()` also returns lag 0, which is always 1, so lag $k$ is element $k + 1$.)

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
autocorrelations <- acf(visits, lag.max = 60, plot = FALSE)$acf
autocorrelations[c(2, ______)]
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
autocorrelations[c(2, 53)]
```

About 0.69 at lag 1 and 0.68 at lag 52, as in the chapter: each week is like the week before, and like the same week a year earlier.
:::
:::

### Exercise 4: The unusual week

Decompose the series with `stl()`, find the week with the largest remainder, and show its date and number of visits.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
decomposition <- stl(visits, s.window = "periodic", robust = TRUE)
plot(decomposition)
remainder <- decomposition$time.series[, "______"]
biggest <- which.max(abs(remainder))
counselling[biggest, ]
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
remainder <- decomposition$time.series[, "remainder"]
```

The week of 23 October 2023, with 71 visits: the mental health awareness week. `s.window = "periodic"` makes the seasonal pattern exactly the same every year, a simpler version of the chapter's STL.
:::
:::

## Forecasting the test year

### Exercise 5: Seasonal naive on the test year

Forecast the fifth academic year with the seasonal naive method (a copy of the fourth year) and with the mean of the first four years, and compare their MAEs. (`year_of(k)` returns the 52 weeks of academic year `k`.)

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
actual <- year_of(5)
snaive_fc <- year_of(______)
mean_fc <- mean(counselling$visits[1:208])
c(snaive = mae(actual, snaive_fc), mean = mae(actual, mean_fc))
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
snaive_fc <- year_of(4)
```

An MAE of about 7.0 visits a week for the seasonal naive forecast, and about 16.3 for the mean: the same values as fable gave in the chapter.
:::
:::

### Exercise 6: A better benchmark

The seasonal naive forecast copies one year's noise, including the awareness week. Average the third and fourth years instead, then multiply by 1.06 to allow for about 6% growth a year. How does the MAE compare with the chapter's STL and ETS model (5.6)?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
actual <- year_of(5)
average_fc <- (year_of(3) + year_of(4)) / 2
growth_fc <- average_fc * ______
c(average = mae(actual, average_fc), with_growth = mae(actual, growth_fc))
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
growth_fc <- average_fc * 1.06
```

About 5.9 for the average of two years, and about 5.7 with growth: almost as good as the STL and ETS model. Averaging smooths away one-off weeks, and the growth factor adds the trend, which is essentially what the model does, estimated from the data rather than chosen by hand.
:::
:::
